CASC Procedures

The Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC) Procedures CASC examines course and program proposals to ensure they are comprehensible and user-friendly for undergraduate students.
Within the Kuali proposal, we examine all ﬁelds to conﬁrm clear details vital to student success, such as prerequisites, course rationale and description, the number of seats and sections offered per year, and syllabi.
Syllabi should accompany all major course proposals (new classes, signiﬁcant modiﬁcations to a course).
To ensure proposal syllabi will be clear to students, we look for: ● straight-forward course information (class description & objectives, method of instruction); ● clear course policies, structures, and methods of teaching; ● clarity regarding grade scale & methods, assignments, and how coursework connects to credit hours; ● current information about accessible technological resources and apps necessary for the class; Further, students are best served by having up-to-date information on support services such as DAI; illness policies; and procedures reﬂecting current University standards.
Where these items are overlooked or out-of-date, CASC may provide friendly feedback.

Also, ATL has resources and templates for syllabi ( https://web.uri.edu/atl/design/syllabus/ ).
New courses should provide supporting documentation uploaded by the chair of the department/academic unit into the proper Kuali ﬁeld, indicating the date that their department/program voted to approve the course.
Program-level proposals should include all materials relevant to the new program/proposed changes, including supporting documentation from other academic units impacted by these changes.
All program and applicable accreditation requirements should be listed .
The Kuali ﬁelds for program proposals should include courses impacted by changes.
Course and Program Overlap Overlap is when a newly proposed or modiﬁed course/program intersects with the content of an existing course or program.
The amount of overlap might range from small (the topics of a single class) to approaching virtual duplication.
Proposers and curriculum approval committees can use search features within Kuali to compare other current and proposed courses/programs for potential overlap.

When CASC recognizes potential overlap, they will ask the course proposer and department/instructor to consult regarding the degree and signiﬁcance of overlap.
Even with substantial replication in content, there might be key differences in approach.
As CASC cannot be experts in all disciplines, we request that the proposer and faculty for the existing course/program work together.
This collaboration can be documented in a statement communicating the resolution to CASC.
If this collaboration cannot occur, CASC exercises its best judgment regarding student beneﬁt.
Note: overlap issues can also be addressed on the Faculty Senate ﬂoor or even at ﬁnal approval with the President.
We also encourage colleges to check for overlap themselves.
Starting in Fall 2025, CASC’s ‘Proposed Temporary and Permanent Courses/Programs’ email will be distributed at the end of the last full week of each month.
We encourage each college’s curriculum committee to meet during the ﬁrst full week of each month and, as part of their deliberations, carefully consider all newly proposed offerings in that CASC newsletter for potential overlap.

Any overlapping courses/programs should be reported to Genviéve Spitale ( genvieve.spitale@uri.edu ); the course/program will not be reviewed until the originating and overlapping colleges agree in writing that either the original proposal or a revised version can move forward for CASC/Gen Ed/Grad Council consideration.

5.10.10 Committees, Boards, Councils and other such entities which have a university-wide function are described in this chapter. With few exceptions, committees with a narrower scope are not included here. For information on them, consult policy documents of various campus units, such as college by-laws, where available, and the Graduate Student Manual. Standing committees of the Faculty Senate, although having university-wide function, can be found in the by-laws of the Faculty Senate.

5.10.11 The committees included here are organized according to the jurisdictional rubric under which they fall, and are divided into (1) committees falling under presidential jurisdiction; (2) committees falling under direct jurisdiction of the general faculty or of the Graduate Faculty; and (3) committees falling under the joint purview of the Faculty Senate and the President. The division into the various jurisdictional rubrics has been proposed by a Faculty Senate Constitution, By-Laws, and University Manual (CBUM) subcommittee on the basis of research conducted during the 2001-02 academic year. This research primarily took into consideration the jurisdictional divide between the President (administration) and the Faculty Senate resulting from Article II of the Senate Constitution; when this was not conclusive, the historic understanding of who had jurisdiction at the time of the establishment of a committee or its predecessor was taken into account. In most cases, these criteria allowed a clear determination of a committee’s jurisdictional rubric. To limit future disputes about jurisdiction, the subcommittee proposed that the Faculty Senate endorse and accept the jurisdictional division resulting from the subcommittee’s research, the senate did so at its meeting on November 11, 2003, and the President endorsed the senate legislation on December 5, 2003.

Members shall serve two-year terms, one-half of the appointments to be made each year, and which may be renewable; the President shall designate the chairperson. 5.23.10 The Institutional Biosafety Committee (IBC) shall review and approve the use of recombinant DNA, synthetic DNA, infectious microorganisms, certain biological toxins, and human or nonhuman blood, unfixed tissues or cells in all research projects and educational activities under the jurisdiction or control of the University. The use of these materials shall be in accordance with the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Guidelines for Research Involving Recombinant or Synthetic Nucleic Acid Molecules and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories as well as any other applicable federal, state and local law. Administrative Report September 2015

5.23.11 The membership shall comprise at least five members appointed by the Vice President of Research and Economic Development selected so that they collectively have experience and expertise in recombinant or synthetic nucleic acid molecule technology and the capability to assess the safety of recombinant or synthetic nucleic acid molecule research and to identify any potential risk to public health or the environment. At least two members shall not be affiliated with the institution (apart from their membership on the Institutional Biosafety Committee) and who represent the interest of the surrounding community with respect to health and protection of the environment. The Vice President for Research and Economic Development or the Vice President’s designee shall serve ex officio , as a non-voting member. An effort will be made to appoint members to the IBC that will have the qualifications of experience and expertise needed to provide guidance and counsel to researchers.

5.24.10 The Conflict of Interest Management Committee (CIMC) is responsible for the review and assessment of all financial disclosures related to research projects at URI and for determining any actions required to ensure that real or perceived financial conflicts of interest are managed or eliminated as required by the RI Public Private Partnership Act as well as any other applicable federal law or policy. Administrative Report September 2015
5.24.11 The membership shall be appointed by the Vice President of Research and Economic Development and shall at a minimum include a public member and a faculty member from an institution of higher education outside the system of public higher education in Rhode Island. The Vice President for Research and Economic Development or the Vice President’s designee shall serve ex officio , as a voting member.

5.25.10 The Institutional Review Board (IRB) shall review and approve all biomedical and behavioral research involving human subjects which is conducted or sponsored by the University. The Code of Federal Regulations, 45 CFR 46, revised in 2005, requires the existence of this committee in order to protect the rights and welfare of the human subjects of such research. See Appendix G for the University’s policy and procedures concerning the protection of human subjects.

5.25.11 The IRB shall comprise at least five members appointed by the President. The chairperson shall be recommended by the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs to the President, to be appointed for one three-year term. Other IRB members shall be appointed for two-year, renewable terms. The IRB shall not consist entirely of men, entirely of women, or entirely of members of one profession. At least one member shall be a person whose primary training and research concerns are in nonscientific areas; for example, lawyers or members of the clergy. At least one member shall be a person who is not otherwise affiliated with the institution or part of the immediate family of a person who is affiliated with the institution. One member shall be a person whose primary training and research concerns are in the scientific area, for example a physician, a biologist, or a psychologist. When research is reviewed involving a category of vulnerable subjects (e.g., prisoners, children, individuals institutionalized as mentally disabled), the IRB shall include at least one member who has as a primary concern the welfare of these subjects. The Vice President for Research and Economic Development or the Vice President’s designee shall serve ex officio , as a non-voting member. An effort will be made to appoint members so that the IRB will be sufficiently qualified through the experience and expertise of its members, the diversity of their racial and cultural backgrounds, and their sensitivity to community attitudes, to be respected for its advice and counsel in safeguarding the rights and welfare of human subjects.

5.25.12 To avoid conflict of interest, an IRB member shall not participate in the IRB’s review of any project in which the member is involved as a researcher or subject.
5.26.10 The Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) shall review and approve the use of vertebrate animals in all research projects, educational or outreach activities under the jurisdiction or control of the University. The procurement, care, and use of animals shall be in accordance with the regulations and terms of the federal Animal Welfare Act as well as any other applicable federal, state and local law.

5.26.11 The IACUC shall be comprised of at least five members appointed by the President including the University of Rhode Island Attending Veterinarian, a scientist experienced in laboratory animal research, a non-scientist and an individual who has no other affiliation with the University besides membership in the IACUC. The Vice President for Research and Economic Development or the Vice President’s designee shall serve ex officio, as a non-voting member. An effort will be made to appoint members to the IACUC that will have the qualifications of experience and expertise needed to provide guidance and counsel to animal researchers.

5.27.10 The Diving Control Board (DCB) has authority over all scientific diving operations at the University of Rhode Island. The DCB sets rules and regulations in compliance with the American Academy of Underwater Sciences standards and in conformance to University policy. All research diving involving equipment or personnel from the University of Rhode Island shall adhere to the rules and regulations which are included in the Research Diving Manual. The Diving Control Board also serves as a search committee for the Diving Safety Officer and provides advice and counsel to the Vice President for Research and Economic Development who makes the appointment.

We are at a unique moment in our history where long-standing struggles of racism, gender inequality, LGBTQ+, socio-economic status, ability, and religious differences are intensified and up for debate in the public and private spheres.
Knowing more about the root causes of the struggles LGBTQ+ individuals experience in the areas of employment, housing, politics, immigration controls, and legal institutions, to name a few, creates an opening for students to engage in systemic change and re-think their lived experiences.
The purpose of this minor is to expose students to histories, theories, concepts, and methods that have contested historical and ongoing harm and oppression.
Students are encouraged to examine their social location, lived experiences, collaborative engagement, and organizing capacity to transform our world by learning how societal structures keep inequality and oppression alive.
The QTS Minor will offer students, especially younger generations, an opportunity to read, discuss, and engage with transnational issues that affect the lives of queer and transgender communities.

Since we live in a transnational world, the QTS minor will allow students to read, think, and analyze social justice issues through an interdisciplinary and intersectional framework.
While the QTS is complementary and overlaps with courses in the GWS, this minor offers an advanced level of proficiency in Queer and Transgender studies, politics, and culture, with a social justice commitment to scholarship, community engagement, and global citizenship.
From participating in interdisciplinary and innovative research, to social activism, to policy work in housing, wage gap, mental and medical services, media coverage, and decriminalization, these are some of the issues in which students will gain exposure, knowledge, and practical experiences to the problems affecting queer and transgender communities.
By broadening the scope of the QTS minor through an interdisciplinary and intersectional framework, students will be able to expand their prospects in the job market.
URI is “one of the top 50 LGBTQ-friendly universities in the nation.” A minor in Queer and Transgender Studies will add to the university’s local and international reputation as a leader for LGBTQ+ students.

While the university and the center for Gender and Sexuality pride themselves on education, support, and engagement for LGBTQ+, no sustained intellectual program caters to students’ needs to study queer and transgender histories.
This minor will fill this educational gap and change the campus community’s climate.
For instance, studies have shown that an increasing number of U.S. adults consider themselves LGBTQ+, with Gen Z representing the large segment of LGBTQ+.
Gallup Poll, Social Services report indicated that at least 54.6% of LGBT Americans identify as bisexual, with Generation Z (1997-2002) representing 15.9% of the U.S. population. [1] The University of Rhode Island Climate Survey indicates that 730 students identify as LGBTQ+, roughly 18.3% of the 4,555 students surveyed.
The minor will attract not only this demographic but offer existing students at URI an intellectual space to explore their lived experiences.

While a growing younger American population identifies or has some experience with same-sex attractions, in 2022, more than 200 anti-LGBT bills were introduced in several states across the U.S. [2] These contradictions reveal a discord between public needs and opponents who continue to push anti-LGBTQ+ legislation.
However, this is not only a U.S.-based issue; similar trends of backlash against LGBTQ+ minorities are occurring in Brazil, Ghana, Russia, and Hungary.
For instance, the Florida "Don't Say Gay" bill was modeled after Hungarian anti-LGBTQ+ bills. [3] There is a global shift towards authoritarianism which seeks to threaten years of marginal gains made by minorities across race, class, gender, sexual, ability, and ethnicity.
The social, political, and economic gains and rights acquired over the last 60 years are subjected to state and national interventions, with growing concerns that minority rights will be rescinded.
Despite the LGBTQ+ population being more visible than ever, there is still systematic discrimination and oppression across post-secondary institutions, civil services, the military, employment, and health care, to name a few.

The education system is vital for bridging students' experiences with existing theories and methods.
Students will be required to complete six courses to receive the minor.
The gateway course 210G: Introduction to Queer and Transgender Studies fulfills the general education requirements of A2, C3, and the grand challenge.
The QTS minor is a unique curriculum, allowing students to develop the knowledge and skills necessary to create positive change.

Students who minor in QTS are eligible for scholarships offered by GWS: the Carlson Single Mother, Carlson Trust, Dorothy Donnelly, and Mother Jones.
Rhode Island College is the only institution in the state that offers a dedicated Queer Studies minor for undergraduates from their Gender & Women’s Studies Program.
Regionally, there are two minor programs in Massachusetts and one in New Hampshire: Brandeis University’s minor in Sexuality and Queer Studies through the Women’s, Gender, and Sexuality Studies program; Bridgewater State University’s GLBT Studies minor, through the College of Humanities and Social Sciences; and University of New Hampshire’s Queer Studies minor.
Hampshire College offers a Queer, Trans, and Sexuality Studies certificate.

Non-degree and non-certificate granting institutions regionally are Yale University, which has a committee on Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender Studies primarily overseeing programming, and Wesleyan University, which promotes, each semester, a course cluster in Queer Studies.
The proposed minor in Queer and Transgender Studies is similar in ethos to the minor offered at RIC.
However, in execution, the proposed minor in Queer and Transgender Studies is more focused and rigorous.
Therefore, we do not anticipate that a minor in Queer and Transgender Studies at URI will compete with the minor offered by RIC.

Compared to students at Rhode Island College, the URI student body draws from a broader population of out-of-state students.
As such, we expect that offering a minor in Queer and Transgender Studies will only add to the attractive programs available at URI for prospective and incoming students choosing among colleges and universities in the region.
A minor in Queer and Transgender Studies, as an interdisciplinary focus not only on LGBTQ lives and communities but also on the social, cultural production, and regulation of gender and sexuality, will complement every major on offer at URI.
Because of its interdisciplinary, intersectional, and transnational understanding of sexual and sexualized desires, identities, communities, and cultures in the US and globally, a minor in Queer and Transgender Studies at URI would be a close complement to existing majors in the humanities, social sciences, and sciences such as Communications, Writing & Rhetoric, English, Sociology, Anthropology, Africana Studies, Film Media, Theatre, Biology, Human Development, and Family Studies, Journalism, Economics, History, and more.

Transgender Activism: This course will introduce the emerging �eld of transgender studies through a look at the history of transgender movements in the United States, focusing on their theoretical analysis and their activist praxis.
We will approach transgender identity through an intersectional framework, emphasizing gender as a social construction that is always enmeshed in larger systems of domination.
Students will gain pro�ciency in contemporary transgender thought and the critical thinking skills needed to understand transgender politics and productively participate in transgender movements. (offered every year, 3 credits) GWS 350.
Queer and Trans Disability Studies: This seminar introduces the key concepts and contentions of disability studies and the disability justice movement through its queer and trans activists and thinkers.

Through theoretical texts, novels, personal narratives, and art created by queer and trans disabled people, we will explore the ways that disabled people are challenging systemic ableism: the devaluing of disabled lives and experiences, disabling structures and systems, and the privileging of normative ways of being.
We will examine the ways that disabled activists and scholars have theorized disability as a part of larger systems of domination, including sexism, capitalism, colonization, and slavery. (offered every year, 3 credits) GWS 350.
Queer Intimacies in the Global South This upper-level seminar takes an interdisciplinary approach to examining “queer intimacies” in the Global South.
Using “queer intimacy” as a heuristic analytic device, we will explore how feelings, emotions, affects, and textures allow us to position intimacy in relation to broader intersectional categories of race, gender, sexuality, nation, and class. ‘Queer Intimacy’ attends to practices that spill out, over, and beyond �xed subjective identities and social, political, and economic structures.

Engaging in course readings through thematic ideas (e.g., domestic home and labor, kinship, migration, etc.,) we will look at queer intimacies in the Global South that became subject to government intervention, colonial reforms, and post-colonial and decolonial movements. (offered every year, 3 credits) GWS 350.

Queer and Feminist Methods: Research methodologies and methods are foundational in advancing our knowledge of the world.
Yet, theories and methods are also domination, power, and control tools.
This interdisciplinary seminar examines non-normative research methodologies as a lens to disrupt dominant knowledge production in the West, centering theories, ideas, and methods from alternative perspectives.

This course will prepare humanities and social sciences students to conduct research.
It will thus provide students with the essential tools to apply social science feminist and queer methods in their study, such as incorporating theory and developing research questions and hypotheses. (Pre: GWS 310 or 315 or 320, and senior standing or permission by the instructor, may count for graduate credit).
